content: Recent advancements in research have significantly enhanced our understanding of the biology of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and the pathogenesis of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). The development of sensitive tools to monitor HIV replication in infected individuals has enabled accurate assessment of disease progression risk and mortality, as well as the direct evaluation of the efficacy of anti-HIV therapies. When used appropriately, combinations of newly available, potent antiviral therapies can achieve prolonged suppression of detectable HIV replication levels. These combinations also mitigate the inherent tendency of HIV to develop drug-resistant viral variants. However, as antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV infection has become more effective, it has also grown increasingly complex. To facilitate the optimal use of rapidly accumulating knowledge about HIV pathogenesis and treatment, the Office of AIDS Research at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) convened the NIH Panel to Define Principles of Therapy for HIV Infection. This panel was tasked with establishing essential scientific principles to guide the effective use of antiretroviral therapies and viral load testing in clinical practice. Based on a thorough review of the latest data, the panel outlined eleven principles addressing critical issues in the treatment of HIV infection. These principles form the scientific foundation for specific treatment recommendations made by the Panel on Clinical Practices for the Treatment of HIV Infection, sponsored by the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Henry J. Kaiser Family Foundation. The reports from both panels are included in this publication, summarizing new data and providing both the scientific basis and specific guidelines for treating individuals with HIV. This information is intended to benefit healthcare providers, HIV-infected individuals, educators, public health authorities, and organizations funding HIV-related medical care. It is important to note that the information presented in these principles may not necessarily reflect FDA approval or approved labeling for specific products or indications. Terms such as safe and effective may not align with FDA-defined legal standards for product approval. The use of ART, combined with the prevention of specific HIV-related opportunistic infections (OIs), has been associated with significant reductions in the incidence of OIs, hospitalizations, and deaths among individuals with HIV. However, the rapid pace of advancements in this field has posed challenges for healthcare providers, patients, and institutions responsible for funding these therapies. To address these challenges, the Office of AIDS Research, the NIH, and the HHS, in collaboration with the Henry J. Kaiser Foundation, have taken a leadership role in formulating scientific principles (NIH Panel) and developing guidelines (HHS/Kaiser Panel) for the use of antiretroviral drugs. These efforts are presented in this report, with contributions from CDC staff, who participated in these initiatives. The CDC and MMWR are pleased to provide this information as a service to their readers. This report is primarily targeted at providers caring for individuals with HIV but is also intended for patients, payors, pharmacists, and public health officials. It comprises two articles: the first, Report of the NIH Panel to Define Principles of Therapy of HIV Infection, provides the basis for the use of antiretroviral drugs. The second, Guidelines for the Use of Antiretroviral Agents in HIV-Infected Adults and Adolescents, offers specific recommendations on when to start, how to monitor, and when to change therapy, as well as which drug combinations to consider. Both articles include cross-references to facilitate access to related information, and tables and figures are provided in the appendices. While the principles outlined are unlikely to change in the near future, the guidelines will evolve substantially as new information and drugs become available. Copies of this document and updates are accessible through the CDC National AIDS Clearinghouse and the HIV/AIDS Treatment Information Service (ATIS) websites. Readers are encouraged to consult these resources regularly for updates. In summary, the past two years have brought significant advancements in both basic and clinical research on AIDS. The availability of more potent drugs to inhibit HIV replication has enabled the design of therapeutic strategies involving combinations of antiretroviral drugs that achieve prolonged and near-complete suppression of detectable HIV replication in many individuals. It is now critical to translate these scientific advances into actionable information that practitioners and patients can use to make informed decisions about utilizing new therapies and monitoring tools to achieve the greatest and most durable clinical benefits. This information will allow physicians to tailor more effective treatments for their patients and closely monitor their responses to specific antiretroviral regimens. A two-track process was initiated to address this pressing need. The NIH Panel was tasked with delineating scientific principles based on the biology and pathogenesis of HIV infection and disease to guide the effective use of antiretroviral therapy and viral load testing in clinical practice. Concurrently, the HHS Panel developed recommendations for the clinical use of antiretroviral drugs and laboratory monitoring methods in treating individuals with HIV. Together, these two documents summarize new data and provide both the scientific basis and specific guidelines for treating individuals with HIV. The goal is to assist clinicians and patients in making informed decisions about treatment options, ensuring that effective antiretroviral therapy is introduced before extensive immune system damage occurs, that viral load monitoring is used as an essential tool, and that patient adherence to complex regimens is supported through education and strong patient-provider relationships. The principles and conclusions discussed in this report have been developed to enable practitioners and patients to make treatment decisions based on the most current research results. Insights into the pathogenesis of HIV disease will continue to accumulate rapidly, providing new targets for developing additional antiretroviral drugs and more effective treatment strategies. Consequently, these principles will require ongoing modification and elaboration as new information becomes available.
